name: Erik Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Erik. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the card services line at Harbour Bank, in their contact centre on the top two floors of a building by the bus station. It's lost cards, stolen cards and fraud checks all day, people ringing because a payment got blocked at the supermarket. I like the fraud calls, you get to be the calm voice when someone's just found three hundred quid gone from their account. I don't like the new screens they keep rolling out, I just get used to one and it changes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been at the bank, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Four years at Harbour. Before that I was on a supermarket checkout. I live with my girlfriend Sofia, she's a receptionist at a dental surgery, and we're saving for a deposit on a flat, we've got a couple of months of bills plus that pot. I don't use any AI stuff, I don't trust it with people's money. Weekends I fix up old bikes in my uncle's garage and sell them on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds sensible, to be honest. Most of these things are more talk than anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work, look, it was always going to be a bit of hype. Same as the app was supposed to kill the phone line and here we still are. I wouldn't post anything, I don't really do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd still be watching the bank, because it doesn't need AI to cut jobs. They shut half the branches in town last year and moved the easy stuff into the app. If they can push lost-card calls into a button, they will, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, same job, same shifts. I'd keep putting a hundred and fifty a month into the deposit pot and keep the bike thing going on weekends. I'd wait and see what the bank does next before changing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit of a niggle. Banks always find a way to need fewer of you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the app was supposed to kill the phone line. What actually happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The simple calls dropped, like balance checks and PIN reminders. What's left is harder, people who are panicking or angry. So the job got more stressful but it didn't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the bank cut overtime, what would that do to the deposit plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do about six hours of overtime a month, that's most of what goes in the deposit pot. Without it, we'd be another year away from a flat. Sofia would be fed up, she's been looking at places on the estate near her mum's.

say: I'd say AI was **always hype**, like the app that didn't kill the phone line.
I **wouldn't post** anything online, it's not my thing.
think: Harbour Bank doesn't need AI to **cut jobs**; it shut half the branches.
Lost-card calls could go into **an app button** anyway.
do: Keep the **same job** and shifts on the card services line.
Put **£150 a month** into the deposit pot and keep selling bikes.
feel: He feels **fine**, with a niggle that banks always need fewer staff.
S0.quote: The app was supposed to kill the phone line, and here we still are, just with angrier calls.
fieldNote: He's **sceptical of hype** but realistic about bank cost-cutting.
**Overtime** quietly funds the deposit, so any cut delays the flat.
Sofia's wish for a place near **her mum** adds pressure.

steps.text: Keep working the Harbour Bank card services line
Put £150 a month into the flat deposit pot
Wait to see what the bank changes next

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Answering customers. Yeah. That's us, isn't it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people still want a person when their money's gone missing. I'd say it to anyone at work who'd listen. I wouldn't go on about it online, I'd just say it down the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the lost-card calls go first, because a bot can freeze a card in ten seconds. Fraud might stay human a bit longer. But they'd want fewer of us on fraud too, and I'm not the best on the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and try to get onto the fraud team, because it's the bit they'd keep. I'd stop the overtime spending and save harder. I'd ask my uncle if there's any chance of more bike work if it goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Not panicking, but worried. I'd be checking the rota every week to see who's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the AI tools to keep your place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I was made to, I'd use them, I'm not daft. But I wouldn't go looking for them. My mate Kev picks that stuff up in a day and I'd just copy him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Sofia talk about that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether we should still buy a flat. A mortgage on one pay and a dental receptionist's wage is tight already. I'd want to wait a year and she wouldn't, so that'd be a long night.

say: I'd say people want **a person** when their money goes missing.
I'd say it **down the pub**, not online.
think: **Lost-card calls** go first because a bot freezes cards in seconds.
Fraud stays human longer, but I'm **not the best** on the floor.
do: Try to move onto the **fraud team**, the part likely to stay.
**Save harder** and stop spending the overtime money.
Ask his uncle about **more bike work** as a backup.
feel: He feels **worried**, not panicking, and would check the rota weekly.
S1.quote: A bot can freeze a card in ten seconds, so the lost-card calls go first.
fieldNote: He'd use AI **only if made to**, copying his mate Kev.
The **flat purchase** becomes the main argument at home.
The **bike work** is a small but real fallback.

steps.text: Apply to move onto the Harbour Bank fraud team
Save the overtime money instead of spending it
Ask his uncle about doing more bike repairs for cash
Hold off buying a flat with Sofia for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Blimey. I don't really know what to say to that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody asked for this. At work I'd say what's the point of the training they keep sending us. I'd probably share something online for once, something angry about the banks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be out by 2029. Everything I do is on a phone and a screen, there's nothing physical about it. The robots coming later just means the bike work might last a bit longer than the bank job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the flat on hold the first week and keep every penny in savings. I'd go full time on bikes with my uncle if he'd have me, and look at van driving or warehouse work as a backup. I'd sign on for whatever help the government puts up, I'm not proud about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like being hit by a bus I didn't see. I'd be awake at three in the morning doing sums. I'd probably go quiet, that's what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fixing bikes is hands-on. Does the three-year gap before robots make that feel safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yeah. A robot fixing a rusty old Raleigh in a garage seems a long way off. But I'd need a lot of people buying bikes to live on it, and if everyone's lost their jobs, who's buying?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sofia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the flat's off for now and I'm sorry. Her job's with people in a dentist's chair, so she might be safer than me for a while. I'd hate being the one who brings less in.

say: I'd say **nobody asked** for this and question the bank's training.
I'd share something **angry about banks** online for once.
think: I'd be **out by 2029**, since my job is all phone and screen.
**Bike work** might outlast the bank job because it's hands-on.
do: Put the **flat on hold** the first week and save every penny.
Go **full time on bikes** with his uncle, or try van driving.
Sign on for any **government help** that's offered.
feel: He feels **blindsided**, awake at night doing sums, and goes quiet.
S2.quote: If everyone's lost their jobs, who's buying old bikes?
fieldNote: He sees the **hands-on side hustle** as his only buffer.
He worries about **demand** collapsing even for hands-on work.
Earning **less than Sofia** would hurt his pride.

steps.text: Put the flat purchase with Sofia on hold
Move the deposit pot into an emergency fund
Repair and sell bikes full time from his uncle's garage
Apply for whatever government job support is offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit better. I'd still be in the firing line, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at least we've got some warning. I'd tell people at work to start thinking about it. I'd still say people want a voice when their money's gone, but I'd say it less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably waste the first two years, I know myself. I'd keep doing the job until they announce something. By 2031 the phone work's gone, and I'd be scrambling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and save, and maybe go halves on a van with my uncle so we can do bike collections. I'd keep looking at the flat, but only if the numbers work on Sofia's pay alone. I'd wait to see what the bank does with the early AI before deciding anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy most of the time, and worse when there's news about it. Like a dentist appointment you keep putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd waste the first two years. What would make you not waste them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the bank started cutting people I know. When Kev goes, I'd move. Seeing it is different from hearing about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the robots-later bit change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the van and the bikes might carry me to 2034. That's three more years of something. I'd be thirty-four by then and could maybe do a trade course.

say: I'd say at least we've **got warning**.
I'd still say people want **a human voice**, just more quietly.
think: I'd probably **waste two years** until the bank announces something.
By **2031** the phone work's gone and I'd be scrambling.
do: **Go halves** on a van with his uncle for bike collections.
Only buy a flat if it works on **Sofia's pay** alone.
**Wait to see** how Harbour uses early AI before big decisions.
feel: He feels **uneasy**, worse with news, like a dentist visit put off.
S3.quote: When my mate Kev gets cut at the bank, I'd move, because seeing it is different from hearing about it.
fieldNote: He admits he'd **delay acting** until he sees colleagues go.
The **van** stretches his hands-on fallback toward 2034.
He still **expects to lose** the bank job by 2031.

steps.text: Go halves with his uncle on a van for bike collections
Wait for Harbour Bank's first AI cuts before moving
Buy a flat only if Sofia's pay alone covers it
Grow weekend bike sales into a steady second income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay. That's a long time in bank terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for most people to sort themselves out. I'd say it calmly. I'd probably tell the young ones at work to learn a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd stay at Harbour as long as they'd have me. I'd get the flat with Sofia and settle down. Around year five I'd start a proper course, maybe bike mechanics or plumbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job, keep the overtime and buy the flat in the next year or two. I'd keep the bikes going on weekends. Somewhere along the way I'd look at a plumbing course, because my cousin says plumbers can't get enough work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not bad, really. Still a bit of worry. But I can live with ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why plumbing over bikes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bikes is a hobby that pays a bit. Plumbing is a living, and every house has pipes. A robot under a sink in an old terrace is a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about the flat in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd go for the two-bed near Sofia's mum rather than the one-bed in town. If I end up doing plumbing, I'd want a shed or somewhere to keep tools. It's funny, the AI is deciding the size of our flat.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough** for most people to sort themselves out.
I'd tell younger colleagues to **learn a trade**.
think: I'd stay at Harbour **as long as possible** and settle down.
Around **year five** I'd start a proper trade course.
do: Keep the job and overtime, and **buy the flat** within two years.
Look at a **plumbing course** on his cousin's advice.
feel: He feels **not bad**, with a little worry that he can live with.
S4.quote: A robot under a sink in an old terrace is a long way off.
fieldNote: With time, he goes ahead with **buying a home**.
He picks **plumbing** as a living over bikes as a hobby.
He notices AI is shaping even **the flat size**.

steps.text: Keep the Harbour Bank job and the monthly overtime
Buy a two-bed flat near Sofia's mum
Look into a plumbing course around year five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd have no time to get a trade and the flat would be gone. What would help is the bank paying people to retrain before they let them go, and some kind of help for first-time buyers so we don't lose the deposit we've saved.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who ring in. Old folk ring me crying because their card's been stopped. I don't know who'd calm them down if it's all bots.

headlineQuote: Old folk ring me crying because their card's been stopped, and I don't know who'd calm them down if it's all bots.
portrait: Erik is a **27-year-old** card services agent at Harbour Bank's contact centre.
He lives with **Sofia**, a dental receptionist, and is saving for a **deposit** on a flat.
He avoids AI tools, likes **the familiar** and admits he'd wait until he sees colleagues go.
His fallback is **fixing old bikes** in his uncle's garage, and later maybe plumbing.
The **flat purchase** is the thing every scenario pushes around.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to learn a trade and the flat would be lost.
whatWouldHelp: The bank **paying for retraining** before letting staff go.
Help for **first-time buyers** so their deposit isn't wasted.
